{{Short description|Fiber bundle whose fibers are projective spaces}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''projective bundle''' is a [[fiber bundle]] whose fibers are [[projective space]]s.

By definition, a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] ''X'' over a [[Noetherian scheme]] ''S'' is a '''P'''<sup>''n''</sup>-bundle if it is locally a projective ''n''-space; i.e., <math>X \times_S U \simeq \mathbb{P}^n_U</math> and transition automorphisms are linear. Over a [[regular scheme]] ''S'' such as a [[smooth variety]], every projective bundle is of the form <math>\mathbb{P}(E)</math> for some vector bundle ([[locally free sheaf]]) ''E''.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. II, Exercise 7.10. (c).}}</ref>

== The projective bundle of a vector bundle ==
Every [[vector bundle]] over a [[Algebraic variety|variety]] ''X'' gives a projective bundle by taking the projective spaces of the fibers, but not all projective bundles arise in this way: there is an [[Obstruction theory|obstruction]] in the [[cohomology group]] ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'',O*). To see why, recall that a projective bundle comes equipped with transition functions on double intersections of a suitable open cover. On triple overlaps, any lift of these transition functions satisfies the cocycle condition up to an invertible function. The collection of these functions forms a 2-cocycle which vanishes in ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'',O*) only if the projective bundle is the projectivization of a vector bundle. In particular, if ''X'' is a compact [[Riemann surface]] then ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'',O*)=0, and so this obstruction vanishes.

The projective bundle of a vector bundle ''E'' is the same thing as the [[Grassmann bundle]] <math>G_1(E)</math> of 1-planes in ''E''.

The projective bundle '''P'''(''E'') of a vector bundle ''E'' is characterized by the universal property that says:<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. II, Proposition 7.12.}}</ref>
:Given a morphism ''f'': ''T'' → ''X'', to factorize ''f'' through the projection map {{nowrap|''p'': '''P'''(''E'') → ''X''}} is to specify a line subbundle of ''f''<sup>*</sup>''E''.
For example, taking ''f'' to be ''p'', one gets the line subbundle ''O''(-1) of ''p''<sup>*</sup>''E'', called the [[tautological line bundle]] on '''P'''(''E''). Moreover, this ''O''(-1) is a [[universal bundle]] in the sense that when a line bundle ''L'' gives a factorization ''f'' = ''p'' ∘ ''g'', ''L'' is the pullback of ''O''(-1) along ''g''. See also [[Cone (algebraic geometry)#O.281.29|Cone#''O''(1)]] for a more explicit construction of ''O''(-1).

On '''P'''(''E''), there is a natural [[exact sequence]] (called the tautological exact sequence):
:<math>0 \to \mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(E)}(-1) \to p^* E \to Q \to 0</math>
where ''Q'' is called the tautological quotient-bundle.

Let ''E'' ⊂ ''F'' be vector bundles (locally free sheaves of finite rank) on ''X'' and ''G'' = ''F''/''E''. Let ''q'': '''P'''(''F'') → ''X'' be the projection. Then the natural map {{nowrap|''O''(-1) → ''q''<sup>*</sup>''F'' → ''q''<sup>*</sup>''G''}} is a global section of the [[sheaf hom]] {{nowrap|Hom(''O''(-1), ''q''<sup>*</sup>G) <nowiki>=</nowiki> ''q''<sup>*</sup> ''G'' ⊗ ''O''(1)}}. Moreover, this natural map vanishes at a point exactly when the point is a line in ''E''; in other words, the zero-locus of this section is '''P'''(''E'').

A particularly useful instance of this construction is when ''F'' is the direct sum ''E'' ⊕ 1 of ''E'' and the trivial line bundle (i.e., the structure sheaf). Then '''P'''(''E'') is a [[hyperplane]] in '''P'''(''E'' ⊕ 1), called the hyperplane at infinity, and the complement of '''P'''(''E'') can be identified with ''E''. In this way, '''P'''(''E'' ⊕ 1) is referred to as the projective completion (or "compactification") of ''E''.

The projective bundle '''P'''(''E'') is stable under twisting ''E'' by a line bundle; precisely, given a line bundle ''L'', there is the natural isomorphism:
:<math>g: \mathbf{P}(E) \overset{\sim}\to \mathbf{P}(E \otimes L)</math>
such that <math>g^*(\mathcal{O}(-1)) \simeq \mathcal{O}(-1) \otimes p^* L.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. II, Lemma 7.9.}}</ref> (In fact, one gets ''g'' by the universal property applied to the line bundle on the right.)

== Examples ==
Many non-trivial examples of projective bundles can be found using fibrations over <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> such as [[Lefschetz fibrations]]. For example, an elliptic [[K3 surface]] <math>X</math> is a K3 surface with a fibration<blockquote><math>\pi:X \to \mathbb{P}^1</math></blockquote>such that the fibers <math>E_p</math> for <math>p \in \mathbb{P}^1</math> are generically elliptic curves. Because every elliptic curve is a genus 1 curve with a distinguished point, there exists a global section of the fibration. Because of this global section, there exists a model of <math>X</math> giving a morphism to the projective bundle<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Propp|first=Oron Y.|date=2019-05-22|title=Constructing explicit K3 spectra|class=math.AT|eprint=1810.08953}}</ref><blockquote><math>X \to \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(4)\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(6)\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1})</math></blockquote>defined by the [[Weierstrass equation]]<blockquote><math>y^2z + a_1xyz + a_3yz^2 = x^3 + a_2x^2z + a_4xz^2 + a_6z^3</math></blockquote>where <math>x,y,z</math> represent the local coordinates of <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(4), \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(6), \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}</math>, respectively, and the coefficients<blockquote><math>a_i \in H^0(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(2i))</math></blockquote>are sections of sheaves on <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>. Note this equation is well-defined because each term in the Weierstrass equation has total degree <math>12</math> (meaning the degree of the coefficient plus the degree of the monomial. For example, <math>\text{deg}(a_1xyz) = 2 + (4 + 6 + 0) = 12</math>).

The [[Contact bundle|contact bundles]], and more generally [[Grassmann bundle|Grassmann bundles]], are projective bundles. The [[unit tangent bundle]] of a [[Riemannian manifold]] is a [[Double cover (topology)|double cover]] of its projectivized [[tangent bundle]].

== Cohomology ring and Chow group ==
Let ''X'' be a complex smooth [[projective variety]] and ''E'' a complex vector bundle of rank ''r'' on it. Let ''p'': '''P'''(''E'') → ''X'' be the projective bundle of ''E''. Then the [[cohomology ring]] H<sup>*</sup>('''P'''(''E'')) is an [[associative algebra|algebra over]] H<sup>*</sup>(''X'') through the pullback ''p''<sup>*</sup>. Then the first [[Chern class]] ζ = ''c''<sub>1</sub>(''O''(1)) generates H<sup>*</sup>('''P'''(''E'')) with the relation
:<math>\zeta^r + c_1(E) \zeta^{r-1} + \cdots + c_r(E) = 0</math>
where ''c''<sub>''i''</sub>(''E'') is the ''i''-th Chern class of ''E''. One interesting feature of this description is that one can ''define'' Chern classes as the coefficients in the relation; this is the approach taken by Grothendieck.

Over fields other than the complex field, the same description remains true with [[Chow ring]] in place of cohomology ring (still assuming ''X'' is smooth). In particular, for Chow groups, there is the direct sum decomposition
:<math>A_k(\mathbf{P}(E)) = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1} \zeta^i A_{k-r+1+i}(X).</math>
As it turned out, this decomposition remains valid even if ''X'' is not smooth nor projective.<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Theorem 3.3.}}</ref> In contrast, ''A''<sub>''k''</sub>(''E'') = ''A''<sub>''k''-''r''</sub>(''X''), via the [[Gysin homomorphism]], morally because that the fibers of ''E'', the vector spaces, are contractible.
